notes: Three more wave-3 monsters fight the way their stories always said they would. The Callback wears the face of someone your village lost — it speaks in their voice, using things they actually said, and fights with their moves. Hold a funeral for them mid-fight — say goodbye properly — and it lets go. Or look it in its too-symmetrical eyes and tell it what it isn't.

Buffering lives three seconds in the past: it tells you exactly what it will do next, and it means it. Its afterimages are the lie — the faintest frame is where it really is. Stand perfectly still and it swings at where you were going to be. Or close your eyes and swing at where it IS.

The Ad Break pauses the whole fight for a sponsored message — a real progress bar, and it heals while you watch. Wait for the skip button (it comes sooner if the audience loves you), look away and starve it of attention, or pop the little sponsor-creature riding the glyph to fast-forward.

Three of the Final Draft’s monsters finally fight the way their stories always said they would. The Redactor points at something you love — your weapon, your footing, even your last turn — a full round before it redacts it into silence; carry a decoy rattle and it takes the loudest thing instead, or go quiet for two turns and it starves.

Gavel holds a real trial: it accuses you from your own history, waits a round, then the verdict falls. You can object (costs fame), demand a recess (once), or confess first (smaller verdict — but everyone remembers). Flank it; frontal attacks hit the sound-block.

The Focus Group rates your every move out loud — loved actions hit harder but get answered, hated ones are safe but weak. Pop its three mouth-heads to end it, or just be boring for three rounds and they’ll wander off.

Three of the Final Draft's monsters fight for real now. The Spool tapes your opening moves and plays them back at you — feed it something harmless (a wait, a bandage) and its replay is useless. The Chorus Line keeps a 4/4 beat you can hear coming — dance through the downbeat, move with it, flank it, or break its rhythm with a handful of gravel. And the Terms of Service will try to get you to sign mid-fight — read the fine print; there's a way out in section zero.

Alien players stay dead now. Kill one and they're gone for good — no more running into the same hunter weeks later sending you packages from beyond the grave. The feed marks the moment with a silence, then the betting resumes.
They've also stopped gloating about kills they didn't make: beat one in a fight and they react like someone who lost, and a dead hunter gives no post-fight speech.

Late-wave monsters now bite through armor the way they were always meant to: the Final Draft's claws find seams, the Mirror Draft's teeth find more, and the Producers barely notice plate at all. Armor still helps — it just isn't a wall anymore past wave 3.

The ground remembers now: forage the same turf too hard and it thins — lush to picked-over to barren. Examine or work a patch to read its state; rested ground comes back, but it takes weeks, not days.
You can farm at the haven: clear a plot, sow seeds from plants you actually know, tend it daily, harvest every few days. A kept garden feeds people. A neglected one dies.
Your neighbors work the same ground. Shared turf thins faster — and they notice. Talk it out at their fire (split the territory, pay tribute, or threaten them), or let it fester into raids.
Fishing got stronger: creeks always hold fish, and a skilled fisher who reads the water sometimes doubles up on the line.

Monsters have learned to hunt parties: hushwolves now run in bigger packs with flanking when three or more of you fight together, hecklers pile onto whoever they shame, and the landlord raises eviction walls to split your group (there's always a service entrance — find it).
The Static has a new trick: it can mimic a crying villager to lure one of your people away from the group. Keep someone close — a hand on the shoulder breaks the spell.

Bright Ideas drift toward bunched-up fighters and the Chorus aims for the densest cluster: spreading out is now a real defense. Solo scouts still get fair duels — the pack only comes out for parties of three or more.

Other villages are alive now, the way yours is. A village you know can split apart — and when it does, the breakaways may walk out of the treeline at dusk and ask for your fire, every one of them named. Your village votes on it at a moot, and the loudest voices on both sides say their piece first. Taking people in means more mouths to feed, and their reputation walks in with them: harbor the eaters and every other fire will remember. You’ll also hear about their hunger, their dead leaders, and their schisms through travelers — late, and not always right. And if a starving village comes begging — or comes with spears — that’s a real choice too.

When something with teeth is at your door, you can call for help four ways now: send a runner (slow, and the road is genuinely dangerous), light the signal fire (fast, but every fire for miles sees it — including the wrong ones), ask the System to carry the call (it's enthusiastic, it mistranslates, and it will collect a favor), or let out an ability cry like a War Cry (fast and honest, if your build earned one). Help arrives as a real party led by a named face from their village — and their foragers leaving their fields is a debt you'll repay, in food or in trust.

Once your village links with another, you can appoint someone to run the relay — the switchboard. Every message in and out passes through their hands, and they can hurry it, sit on it, or rewrite it. Choose carefully: your best talker costs the moots their voice, your weakest forager costs you the village's mood, and a schemer with the relay is a story waiting to happen. Watch the log.

Haven can grow now: stockpile food, wood, stone and preserved food and the village raises the Longhouse (room for 16), the Palisade (room for 20 — walls that bleed raiders and keep your sleep safe), and the Granary (room for 24, slower spoilage, a deeper famine reserve). The System tells you exactly what each one costs, the Haven panel shows your progress, and the village talks about what's missing.

The woods have teeth at night now: when monsters gather and the pantry smells rich, raiders hit Haven. Villagers fight them off for real — and anything they don't meet eats from your stores. There's a new stone-gathering job for the building pile.

Going national is no longer just lead-or-bow: you can confederate as equals — no throne, just a shared granary and a war-pact where every fire answers every call — or found a trade league that pays weekly tariffs but owes no swords. You can also take villages by force now: muster a war party, offer terms, or burn and subjugate — but blood has a price, and conquered fires can rise. And if the System offers you a polity, you can refuse the scale entirely: keep every kcal, answer to no one — and face the late waves alone.
Fan care packages are curios again, never dinner: the mislabeled BEANS can has stopped showing up in fan mail (the galaxy still thinks it is hilarious, it just stopped mailing it).

The wild got deeper: three new waves of monsters are out there now — the Final Draft, the Mirror Draft (built out of us), and the Producers themselves. They arrive when your deeds earn them, not on a schedule. One of them eats. It gets stronger every time it does.

The world got bigger: villages can now grow into something more. Lead a polity of allied villages — or swear yourself to one — and the System starts treating you like a power. Go far enough and the whole world starts watching.
The table got honest: humanity’s case is made of deeds now, not words. Waves fought, contests survived, standing earned, crises weathered — the invitation only comes when the case is real.

New on the title screen: Records. Every run feeds a permanent record of what you’ve encountered — plants, animals, monsters, milestones. New games still start fresh; the record is the reason to play again.

Fishing is honest now: your line catches real fish from the creek’s actual stock — creek chub and bluegill at their real size — and a fished-out creek tells you so instead of biting forever. Ponds hold smaller fish, like the water says.

The bear is a proper fight now. It mauls you every time you swing at close range — a spear's reach still halves it, but a knife up close is answered in full, every time. And if the bear puts you down, you stay down: no more walking away from 0 health.

Issue Challenge dares have real stakes now: if it comes to blows, the village holds you both to the terms — witnessed, to yield. Winner takes respect, loser takes humility. Break the terms with a killing and the village names you oathbreaker.
A delivered ratings stunt really moves the ratings now: when you give the galaxy its moment, the numbers tick up for real — and the System won't drag you back on camera off the same slump twice.
Watching the village's shows together pays what it promises: the good-snacks watch party brings the village closer exactly once, no hidden double-counting.
